{{Short description|American chemist (1942-2025)}}
'''Charles P. Casey''' (January 11, 1942{{snd}}December 21, 2025) was an [[organometallic chemistry|organometallic chemist]] who was the 2004 President of the [[American Chemical Society]].  He was the [[Homer Burton Adkins|Homer Adkins]] Professor Emeritus of Chemistry at the [[University of Wisconsin-Madison]].<ref>{{cite web | title = Charles Casey | publisher = [[American Chemical Society]] | accessdate = 19 August 2015 | url = http://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/policy/acsonthehill/briefings/researchdirections/charles-casey-biography.html}}</ref>  He was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 1993.<ref name=NAS>{{cite web|title=Member directory: Charles P. Casey|url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/charles-p-casey-uaw1rb/|publisher=National Academy of Sciences|access-date=26 August 2015}}</ref>

==Education==
Casey received his B.S. in Chemistry from [[Saint Louis University (United States)|St. Louis University]] in 1963, and his Ph.D. in Chemistry from [[MIT]] in 1967 under the direction of [[George M. Whitesides]].<ref name=AMWS/>  His thesis title was "Thermal decomposition of organocopper(I) compounds".<ref name=tree>{{cite web |url=http://academictree.org/chemistry/peopleinfo.php?pid=55642 |title=Charles P. Casey |publisher=Chemistry Tree}}</ref>  He was then a postdoctoral fellow in organic chemistry at [[Harvard University]] from 1967-1968.<ref name=AMWS>{{cite book|title=American Men & Women of Science|date=2009|publisher=Gale|location=Farmington Hills, MI|isbn=978-1-4144-3302-8|page=103|edition=26th}}</ref>

==Academic career==
Casey's research program focused on the [[Reaction mechanism|mechanisms]] of [[Homogeneous catalysis|homogeneously catalyzed reactions]], and creating new reagents for organic synthesis including [[Heterobimetallic catalysis|heterobimetallic catalysts]].<ref name=NAS/>  More recently, his research had included studies of diruthenium hydrogenation catalysts, which contain both a [[protic]] and a [[hydridic]] hydrogen, and [[hydroformylation]] reaction catalyzed by chelating [[diphosphine]]s with large P-M-P angles.<ref name=caseyweb/>

Casey had been a member of the faculty of the Department of Chemistry at the University of Wisconsin since 1968.  He achieved the rank of Full Professor in 1977.  Named positions he has held at Wisconsin include the Romnes Faculty Fellowship (1977), the Evan P. Helfaer Professorship (1985-1991), and the [[Homer Burton Adkins|Homer B. Adkins]] Professorship (2004–present).<ref name=AMWS /> Among the significant awards he had received for his research are the [[American Chemical Society]] Award in [[Organometallic Chemistry]] in 1991, and the American Chemical Society Award for the Advancement of [[Inorganic Chemistry]] in 2011.<ref name=caseyweb>{{cite web|title=Charles P. Casey|url=https://www.chem.wisc.edu/users/casey|website=UW Madison Department of Chemistry|publisher=[[University of Wisconsin–Madison]]|accessdate=19 August 2015}}</ref>

Casey's advisees include [[Steven H. Bertz]], [[Joseph M. O'Connor]], [[R. Morris Bullock]], [[Seth Marder|Seth R. Marder]], [[Ross A. Widenhoefer]], [[William D. Jones (chemist)|William D. Jones]], [[Richard F. Jordan]], [[Robert E. Colborn]], [[L. Keith Woo]], and [[Jon A. Tunge]].<ref name=tree/>

==Death==
Casey died on December 21, 2025.<ref>{{Cite web | title=Charles Phillip Casey Obituary December 21, 2025 - Cress Funeral and Cremation Services | url=https://www.cressfuneralservice.com/obituaries/charles-casey | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251229083633/https://www.cressfuneralservice.com/obituaries/charles-casey | archive-date=2025-12-29 | access-date=2026-10-10}}</ref>
